patterns.title: Design Patterns
patterns.subtitle: 23 classic Gang of Four patterns
patterns.page_subtitle: All 23 classic Gang of Four patterns for object-oriented software design.
patterns.intro_p1: A design pattern is a general, battle-tested solution to a problem that recurs often in software design. It isn't ready-made code - it's a reusable template you adapt to your own situation.
patterns.intro_p1b: The idea comes from architecture: in 1977, architect Christopher Alexander described recurring solutions for building towns and buildings as a "pattern language" - each entry being a problem, the context it shows up in, and a proven solution. In 1994 the "Gang of Four" applied the same approach to object-oriented programming.
patterns.intro_authors: All 23 patterns come from the book "Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software" (1994) - its authors, Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides, became known as the "Gang of Four" (GoF), and the book is still the standard reference for object-oriented design vocabulary.
patterns.intro_authors_b: Every pattern in the book follows the same template: name, problem it solves, motivation, applicability, class structure, participants, consequences (trade-offs), and a sample implementation. This site follows the same structure for each of the 23 patterns.
patterns.intro_p2_lead: The patterns fall into three groups:
patterns.intro_p2_creational: Creational patterns hide the logic behind object creation, letting a program decide at runtime which class to instantiate instead of hard-coding it.
patterns.intro_p2_structural: Structural patterns show how to assemble classes and objects into larger structures while keeping them loosely coupled and easy to change later.
patterns.intro_p2_behavioral: Behavioral patterns describe how objects split up responsibilities and communicate, reducing tight coupling and making interactions more predictable.
patterns.intro_p3: Knowing these patterns helps developers speak a shared vocabulary, read unfamiliar code faster, and reach for proven solutions instead of reinventing the wheel.
patterns.intro_p4: A pattern is not a goal in itself and not a sign of "correct" code. Applying one where the problem doesn't call for it just adds unnecessary abstraction. Reach for a pattern when it actually solves a problem you have, not because it's "the proper way" to do things.

category_desc.creational: Deal with object creation mechanisms, aiming to create objects in a manner suitable to the situation.
category_desc.structural: Deal with object composition, creating relationships between objects to form larger structures.
category_desc.behavioral: Deal with communication between objects, defining how objects interact and distribute responsibility.
